analysis.one_liner: Keeps Medicare barred from negotiating prescription drug prices and blocks testing of negotiation models.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill, backed by one sponsor and one cosponsor, never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put the Senate on record that Medicare must keep its current ban on negotiating drug prices for the Medicare Part D benefit, and would forbid the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation from even testing a program model that would lift that ban. In other words, it would lock in a system where private drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers negotiate with drug makers, and the government itself never does. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who keep the statutory guarantee that no government negotiator will ever sit across the table from them on Medicare Part D, preserving their power to set prices. Private Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers also benefit, because the bill keeps them in place as the only parties negotiating drug prices. The bill's stated benefit to seniors is preserving wide drug choice: its findings argue that a government-run formulary like the VA's would cover a smaller share of the top Part D drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Brand-name drug makers and drug plans

how_it_helps.text: Declares the sense of the Senate that the 'non-interference' clause — the law barring Medicare from negotiating Part D drug prices or setting a formulary — should not be repealed.

Prohibits the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation from testing any payment or delivery model that would repeal or require a waiver of the non-interference clause, closing off one route Medicare officials had used to pilot program changes.

The bill's findings argue Medicare Part D has come in under cost estimates because of private-market negotiation, and cite an analysis that 74% or more of the top 200 Part D brand-name drugs were covered by private drug plans versus 52% by the VA formulary.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and Medicare beneficiaries, who would continue paying prices set without a government negotiator — the arrangement the bill protects is the one in which the largest drug buyer in the country is forbidden by law from bargaining. Beneficiaries could also face the trade-off the bill itself acknowledges elsewhere: if government negotiation ever came with access restrictions, patients could see narrower formularies.

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently bar Medicare — the largest purchaser of prescription drugs in the United States — from using its bargaining power to lower Part D prices, keeping net drug prices and federal drug spending higher than they might otherwise be.
It would strip the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation of the ability to even test a model involving negotiation, foreclosing experimentation rather than weighing it on the results.

The findings it rests on lean on research and analysis from industry-linked sources, including an analysis by Xcenda (a consulting arm of a drug manufacturer) and patient-satisfaction surveys, while the CBO position it cites — that negotiation alone would yield negligible savings — was disputed by advocates of negotiation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine argument — that a restrictive government formulary could limit seniors' drug choices, as the VA system does — is a real trade-off, and beneficiary satisfaction with Part D is high. But the bill does not strike that balance; it removes the choice entirely by forbidding Medicare from negotiating or even testing negotiation, at a cost of leaving drug prices for tens of millions of beneficiaries and for the federal budget to be set without the government's bargaining power. The prescription-drug pricing legislation that moved in this Congress went the opposite direction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2021, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on April 14, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
It had a single cosponsor, a Republican, and no other senators signed on.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no floor consideration — through the end of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, drug manufacturers did not get an additional statutory lock on the ban against Medicare price negotiation, and the innovation center kept its legal authority to test models. No new barrier to negotiation was created; the existing ban remained as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers failed to lock in the ban

for.name: Pharmaceutical industry
for.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their lobbying groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned to preserve the Medicare Part D 'non-interference' clause, the policy this bill would entrench.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it received no markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, no Democrats signed on, and the bill defended the non-negotiation status quo against the drug-price negotiation proposals pressed by Senate Democrats in the same Congress.

industries.note: The bill would write the ban on Medicare negotiation into Senate policy and forbid the innovation center from testing any model that lifts it, permanently protecting manufacturers' ability to set prices with no government negotiator across the table. Their interest here runs against beneficiaries and taxpayers, who bear the resulting higher prices.

industries.industry: Private Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill locks in private plans and PBMs as the only parties negotiating Part D drug prices, preserving their role and rebate revenue. They argue they deliver broad drug choice, but keeping the government alternative off the table also protects their middleman position.
